cards.title: THE GARAGE
cards.tagline: SEVEN ZONES. START WITH THE BENCH.
cards.objective: The garage takes what every other room in the house evicts, and it carries three problems no other room has all at once: fuel and garden chemicals stored a few feet from where a car parks, heavy bins stacked overhead above where people walk and park, and edged power tools within reach of a child's hand. This card is the map and the order.
zones_in_order: GAZ-002 Hand Tool Wall and Cabinets
GAZ-003 Power Tool and Battery Zone
GAZ-006 Lawn and Garden Tool Zone
cards.start_here: GAZ-001 Primary Workbench. Start with the workbench, not the pile inside the door. A cleared bench top gives you somewhere to lay out the contents of a bin while you judge them, and it is the one part of the garage that pays you back the same afternoon. The slab comes last, once the wall rails and the overhead racks have taken what belongs on them.
how_to_play: 1. Deal the seven ZONE cards face up. Pick the one that is annoying you today, or take the one this card says to start at.
2. Lay out that zone's FRICTION cards. Keep the ones that are true in your garage. Put the rest back.
3. Turn a friction card over and pick the answer that is true. It names a ROOT CAUSE.
4. The root cause card names the ACTION cards that fix that cause. Pick the one that matches the time you actually have: fifteen or thirty minutes.
5. Do it standing up, with the card in your hand.
6. Read the victory condition out loud. If it is not true yet, you are not finished, and that is the whole scoring system.
7. Fill in the zone's STANDARD card with a pen and put it where the zone is.
8. Draw an EVENT card when an ordinary hard day happens, and see whether the standard held.
cards.players: 1 to 4. With more than one, split the chain: one clears the bench and tool wall, another works the power tools and the overhead rack.
cards.six_s: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, Sustain
cards.safety_first: Do GAA-015 The Fuel-and-Chemistry Walk before any rebuild. It takes thirty minutes and covers what makes this room different from every other: fuel, lithium packs and garden chemicals a few feet from where the car parks.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: Chisels, utility knives, and handsaws loose in the bench drawer or lying edge-up on the top where you sweep with a bare hand.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: Rags soaked with oil, stain, or solvent left balled in an open bin under the bench. They can heat on their own with no flame anywhere near them.

the_call.title: The project that has been there since spring
the_call.text: Name the half-finished thing sitting on your bench right now. It gets one of three verdicts today: a specific weekend written on it to finish it, a breakdown that returns the timber, hardware, and hinges to stock, or the skip. The rule that settles it is that anything which has sat untouched through one full season is not a project any more, it is furniture with your intentions stacked on top. Do not solve this by lifting it onto a shelf. That only moves the decision somewhere darker and costs you the bench in the meantime, which is the one surface the whole garage depends on.

the_call.title: The third hammer
the_call.text: You almost certainly own three claw hammers, four adjustable wrenches, and a fistful of Phillips drivers, and the reason you have never thinned them is that each one, held on its own, still works. Working is not the test. The test is which one your hand actually goes to. Keep that one, plus exactly one deliberate spare parked where a second person would need it, the kitchen drawer or the boot of the car. Every remaining duplicate goes today to a friend, a tool library, or the metal skip. A hammer you keep because it still works and never choose is taking the hook that would have made the hammer you love findable in one glance from the door.

the_call.title: The tool whose batteries no longer exist
the_call.text: Somewhere on that shelf is a good tool on a dead platform: the drill from the brand you left behind, one tired pack, and a charger nobody makes any more. You keep it because the tool itself is fine, and it is. Decide this with money rather than loyalty. Price one replacement pack today. If a pack costs more than half what a current equivalent tool costs, or you cannot buy one at all, the tool is finished, so sell it with its charger while it still means something to somebody, or take it to electrical recycling. Running two battery systems is a cost you can defend. Running three means a hunt through three shelves every time you want to put a hole in a wall.

the_call.title: The fluids for the car you no longer own
the_call.text: The hardest bottles here are the two thirds full ones. They cost real money, they have not gone off, and they fit nothing on your driveway. The rule is that every bottle must match a vehicle parked at this address, and no match means no keep. Offer them this week to the neighbour who drives that model, and take whatever is unclaimed to your council's household hazardous waste collection, never down a drain. Then write the opened date on every bottle from today onward, because the only reason this shelf grew this deep is that nobody could tell which ones were still good, so nothing was ever thrown out.

the_call.title: The gear from the sport you stopped playing
the_call.text: Skis, golf clubs, a good tent, the road bike. Each was expensive, each still works, and each stands for a version of your week that has not actually happened in years. That is what makes this the slowest shelf in the garage, and no amount of restacking will settle it. The rule is two full seasons of the right weather with no use, which means you are not on a break, you have stopped. Sell it while the bindings and the groupset are still current, or hand it to someone just starting out, which is a better ending than a decade under a dust sheet. The one exception worth honouring is a named date: if you can finish the sentence "I will use this on ___", keep it and write that date on the bin. If you cannot finish the sentence, it goes this month.

the_call.title: The half-used chemicals
the_call.text: The shelf holds a bag of feed with the top rolled over, a jug of concentrate that moved here from your last house, and something in an unlabelled sprayer that you are fairly confident is weed killer. Start with the unlabelled one, because it is the easy call: you cannot safely use what you cannot name, so it goes to hazardous waste this month without being opened again. For the rest, apply one season of intent. If you will not genuinely use it before the next growing season ends, you are storing a poison above your children's heads for no reason. Take it to a hazardous waste day, or offer it to a neighbour in its own labelled container. Never pour any of it down a drain, into a gutter, or onto the ground behind the shed.

the_call.title: The box you have never opened
the_call.text: There is at least one box up there that moved in with you and has not been opened since. You keep it because opening it costs an afternoon and might cost more than that. Here is what settles it. Bring it down, open it on the floor with three things beside you: a rubbish sack, a donation box, and one empty container. Whatever you truly want to keep has to fit inside that single container and has to have a living person's name attached to it. Anything you cannot name an owner for goes today. Do not tape it up and send it back overhead, because a box that goes back unopened has just bought itself another five years and taught the rack that this is allowed.

cards.title: CLEAR THE BENCH TO THE VISE AND THE LIGHT
cards.tagline: 15 MINUTES. 1.
cards.objective: Clear the bench top down to the vise and the task light, put the current job in one tray, rack the clamps, and sweep until concrete shows underneath.
cards.why_it_matters: A bench with no boundary on what belongs there is why the next job never gets a clear surface to start on, and 'I might need it later' is not the same test as 'this is today's job.'
inputs: a tray for the current job
steps: Clear the bench top down to the vise and the task light, put the current job in one tray, rack the clamps on the rail, and sweep until you can see concrete under the bench.
Wipe the vise screw and give it a drop of oil before you close up.
Check the bench outlet and task light cord for nicks while you're down there.

steps: Mark or tape off the vise's own corner with a full arm's length of open top in front of it.

Carry anything that isn't a bench tool, like a parcel or a paint tin, to the zone it actually belongs to.
Agree who ends each session with the sweep, tied to unplugging the bench outlet.

cards.title: ONE SHELF PER SYSTEM, EVERY GUARD DOWN
cards.tagline: 15 MINUTES. 1.
cards.objective: Give each battery system its own shelf, pull every pack off its charger, and settle every tool into its case or hook with the guard down.
cards.why_it_matters: A pack left sleeping on a charger is the one habit in this room whose failure cannot be undone by tidying afterward, and mixing platforms on one shelf is why the wrong pack keeps going to the wrong tool.
inputs: labelled hooks or bins for each system
steps: Give each battery system one shelf, mount its charger at the front edge, take every pack off every charger, put each tool in its case or on a labelled hook with guards down, and put the bits and blades in the shallow drawer.

cards.if_it_failed: If you had to dig past off-season bins or question the helmet, the sports standard was not being kept. Draw GAA-009 or GAA-010.

cards.title: THE FIRST FROST OF THE SEASON
cards.tagline: THE DAY THAT TESTS IT.

cards.held_if: The hose comes straight off its reel by the door, and every long tool is already off the wet ground and on the rail.
cards.if_it_failed: If a tool was found leaning in a corner, or the hose was tangled on the slab, the lawn and garden standard was not being kept. Draw GAA-011 or GAA-012.

cards.title: THE NEIGHBOUR'S ROOF-LEAK SCARE
cards.tagline: THE DAY THAT TESTS IT.
cards.objective: A neighbour's roof leaked and you want to check your own overhead bins for water damage tonight, without a ladder mishap in the dark.
cards.held_if: Every label reads from the slab, the map by the light switch says exactly which bay to check first, and the heaviest bins are already low enough to check without climbing.
cards.if_it_failed: If you had to climb blind or guess which bin was which, the overhead standard was not being kept. Draw GAA-013 or GAA-014.
